examShortTricks: Trick 1: One formula family: l = l0(1 + αΔT); Δl = l0αΔT. Given any three of l, l0, α, ΔT, substitute directly — always keep temperatures in the SAME scale (difference is same in °C and K).
Trick 2: α of the material decides the gap problem: a rod expands Δl = lαΔT; if a gap is smaller than Δl the rod buckles — classic 2-mark reasoning.
Trick 3: For a pendulum, length increase slows the clock: T ∝ √l; quote 'pendulum clocks lose time in summer' as the application.
keyPoints: Linear expansion: Δl = l0 α ΔT, α = coefficient of linear expansion.
Area expansion: ΔA = 2α A0 ΔT; volume: ΔV = 3α V0 ΔT (β = 3α).
Applications: bimetallic strips, expansion gaps in rails and bridges.
practiceQuestions: Q. A steel rod is 1 m at 0 °C; α = 1.2 × 10^-5 K^-1. Find its length at 40 °C. (2 marks) — l = 1(1 + 1.2e-5 × 40) = 1.00048 m.
Q. Why are small gaps left between railway rails? (1 mark) — to allow thermal expansion in summer without buckling.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Define in one line: heat transfer by actual movement of fluid particles (density change with temperature) — the word 'actual movement' separates it from conduction.
Trick 2: Natural vs forced: natural convection is density-driven (sea breeze, room heater); forced uses a pump/fan — one example pair earns both marks.
Trick 3: Newton's law of cooling: dQ/dt = k(θ − θ0) — quote for the quantitative side and the 'rate proportional to temperature difference' phrase.
keyPoints: Convection: heat carried by the bulk motion of the fluid itself.
Hot fluid expands, becomes lighter and rises; cooler fluid sinks — a convection current.
Natural convection needs no external agency; forced convection uses fans/pumps.
Cannot occur in solids; needs a fluid medium.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why do liquids and gases mainly transfer heat by convection? (1 mark) — their particles can move freely; conduction is poor in fluids.
Q. What creates a sea breeze? (2 marks) — land heats faster; warm air over land rises, cool sea air flows in to replace it.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Four properties in exam order — needs no medium, travels at light speed, obeys inverse-square law, can pass through vacuum — the first property is the definition mark.
Trick 2: Stefan's law numerical: P = σAeT^4, σ = 5.67 × 10^-8 — doubling the absolute temperature multiplies radiation 16 times.
Trick 3: Ideal radiator = ideal absorber = black body (a = 1); a good reflector is a poor radiator — one line, and Kirchhoff's law ties them.
keyPoints: Radiation: heat transfer by electromagnetic waves without a material medium.
Stefan–Boltzmann: P = σ A e T^4.
A black body is both the best absorber and the best radiator (Kirchhoff's law).
Wien's law: λm T = constant — hotter bodies radiate shorter wavelengths.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is a thermos flask's silvered surface used? (1 mark) — to minimise heat loss by radiation (poor radiator/absorber).
Q. By what factor does radiated power increase if absolute temperature doubles? (2 marks) — 2^4 = 16 times (Stefan's law).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Molecular picture in four points: matter made of molecules, intermolecular spacing decides state, molecules attract each other, molecules are in random motion whose KE measures temperature.
Trick 2: State differences by spacing and force: solid — close, strong force, fixed position; liquid — close, weaker, mobile; gas — far apart, negligible force, free motion.
Trick 3: Brownian motion and diffusion are the two EVIDENCES of molecular motion to quote if asked 'how do we know molecules move'.
keyPoints: Molecules are in continuous random motion; their average KE ∝ absolute temperature.
Intermolecular forces and spacing distinguish solids, liquids and gases.
Brownian motion and diffusion evidence molecular motion.
At absolute zero molecular motion is minimum.
practiceQuestions: Q. What happens to molecular motion as temperature rises? (1 mark) — average kinetic energy increases proportionally to absolute temperature.
Q. Give two evidences of molecular motion. (1 mark) — Brownian motion; diffusion.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Constants: kB = R/NA = 1.38 × 10^-23 J/K — one derivation line earns the mark.
Trick 2: rms speed formulas — vrms = √(3RT/M) = √(3kBT/m); lighter gas → faster molecules (H2 vs O2 ratio √16 = 4).
Trick 3: Average KE per molecule = (3/2)kBT — depends ONLY on temperature, not on the gas; that line answers 'why do all gases at the same T have the same average KE'.
keyPoints: Boltzmann constant kB = R/NA = 1.38 × 10^-23 J K^-1.
vrms = √(3kBT/m) = √(3RT/M).
Mean kinetic energy of a molecule = (3/2) kBT.
At fixed temperature lighter molecules move faster.
practiceQuestions: Q. Find the rms speed of O2 molecules at 27 °C (M = 32 g/mol). (3 marks) — v = √(3 × 8.314 × 300/0.032) ≈ 484 m/s.
Q. Compare rms speeds of H2 and O2 at the same temperature. (1 mark) — v(H2)/v(O2) = √(32/2) = 4.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Index chain: n21 = 1/n12; absolute n = c/v — combine to get n1 v1 = n2 v2 and n1 sin i = n2 sin r (Snell).
Trick 2: Denser → rarer: light bends away from normal; speed and wavelength increase, FREQUENCY unchanged — 'frequency never changes' is the 1-mark trap.
Trick 3: Numerical shortcut: n2 = n1 × (v1/v2); with λ: n1 λ1 = n2 λ2.
keyPoints: Refractive index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1: n21 = sin i/sin r = v1/v2.
Absolute refractive index n = c/v.
n21 = n2/n1; reciprocal relations hold between pairs.
On refraction, frequency stays constant; speed and wavelength change.
practiceQuestions: Q. Light goes from glass (n = 1.5) to water (n = 1.33). Find n_wg. (2 marks) — n_wg = 1.33/1.5 = 0.887.
Q. Speed of light in a medium of n = 2? (1 mark) — v = c/n = 1.5 × 10^8 m/s.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The four-step answer earns full marks — bring charged rod NEAR (not touching) → charges separate in the sphere → earth the far side (opposite charge escapes... same sign as rod escapes) → remove earth, then remove rod; sphere is left with charge OPPOSITE to the rod.
Trick 2: Sign rule: the induced charge on the NEAR side has the same sign as the charging body; the far side (and the final charged body after earthing) has the opposite sign.
Trick 3: Induction needs NO contact and leaves the charging body's charge unchanged — contrast with charging by conduction.
keyPoints: Charging by induction: charge a body without contact by rearranging charges with a nearby charged body.
Earthing during induction lets like charge escape, leaving opposite charge.
The charged rod neither loses nor gains charge.
Explains why a rubbed rod attracts neutral paper bits.
practiceQuestions: Q. Describe charging a metal sphere negatively by induction with a positively charged rod. (3 marks) — rod near sphere; earth far side (electrons flow in); remove earth, then rod; sphere negative.
Q. Why does a charged rod attract uncharged paper? (1 mark) — induction polarises the paper; opposite induced charge is nearer, so attraction wins.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: With dielectric fully filling the gap: C = Kε0A/d (capacitance multiplies by K); V falls by K for the same charge; E falls by K — three consequences in one line each.
Trick 2: Polarisation in one sentence: dielectric molecules align their dipole moments against the field, producing an induced surface charge that partially cancels the applied field.
Trick 3: Battery connected vs disconnected: battery keeps V constant (Q changes by K); disconnected keeps Q constant (V falls by K) — the standard conceptual trap.
keyPoints: Dielectric constant K = C_dielectric/C_vacuum.
Polarisation: induced dipoles create an opposing internal field E/K.
With dielectric inserted: C increases K-fold; E and V decrease K-fold at fixed Q.
Energy stored falls by K at fixed charge; rises by K at fixed voltage.
practiceQuestions: Q. A capacitor is charged and disconnected; a dielectric (K = 4) is inserted. What happens to V and E? (2 marks) — both fall 4 times; charge unchanged.
Q. Why does a dielectric increase capacitance? (1 mark) — polarisation reduces the effective field, so more charge fits per volt.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Law statement with condition: V ∝ I at constant temperature — 'constant temperature' is the scoring phrase because resistance drifts when hot.
Trick 2: R = ρl/A; conductivity σ = 1/ρ — combine to R = l/(σA); every wire numerical is one substitution.
Trick 3: Stretching a wire to n times its length: R multiplies by n² (length n, area 1/n) — the classic 2-mark numerical.
Trick 4: V–I graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R.
keyPoints: Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature.
Resistance R = ρ l/A; resistivity ρ is a material property.
Conductivity σ = 1/ρ; unit siemens per metre.
Resistance increases with temperature for metals.
practiceQuestions: Q. A wire is stretched to double its length. What happens to its resistance? (2 marks) — R' = 4R (length doubles, area halves).
Q. Find R of a 2 m copper wire, A = 1 mm², ρ = 1.7 × 10^-8 Ωm. (2 marks) — R = 1.7e-8 × 2/1e-6 = 0.034 Ω.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Definitions in one line each — isotopes: same Z, different A (1H, 2H, 3H); isotones: same N; isobars: same A — three terms, three examples.
Trick 2: Isotopes have identical CHEMICAL properties (same electron configuration) but different physical/mass properties — the contrast is the 2-mark answer.
Trick 3: Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1/12 mass of C-12 = 1.66 × 10^-27 kg; atomic mass ≈ mass number in u.
keyPoints: Isotopes: same proton number, different neutron number.
Isobars: same mass number; isotones: same neutron number.
Isotopes share chemical properties; nuclear properties differ.
practiceQuestions: Q. Distinguish isotopes and isobars with one example each. (2 marks) — 1H/2H/3H isotopes; 14C and 14N isobars.
Q. Why do isotopes of an element show the same chemical behaviour? (1 mark) — identical electronic configuration (same Z).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Intrinsic = PURE Si/Ge: electrons and holes equal (n = p), conductivity rises with temperature (negative temperature coefficient) — opposite to metals.
Trick 2: Extrinsic = DOPED: pentavalent (As, Sb) → n-type (electrons majority); trivalent (B, In) → p-type (holes majority) — one line each with an example dopant.
Trick 3: Both types are NEUTRAL overall — doping adds atoms, not net charge; the common misconception is the mark.
keyPoints: Intrinsic semiconductor: pure crystal, n = p, few charge carriers.
Doping with pentavalent impurity gives n-type (electrons majority).
Doping with trivalent impurity gives p-type (holes majority).
Extrinsic conductivity is far higher and doping-controlled.
practiceQuestions: Q. What happens when Si is doped with arsenic? (2 marks) — n-type; each As donates a free electron (four bonds + one spare).
Q. Are n-type semiconductors negatively charged? (1 mark) — no; they are electrically neutral (electrons balanced by fixed donor ions).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Parallel plate formula C = ε0A/d with the three levers: bigger area ↑C, smaller gap ↑C, dielectric K ↑C — most conceptual questions reduce to these.
Trick 2: Combination rule by analogy with resistors INVERTED: capacitors in parallel ADD (C = C1 + C2); in series reciprocals add (1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2).
Trick 3: In series every capacitor holds the SAME charge; in parallel all share the SAME voltage — decide which rule to apply from this.
Trick 4: Energy U = Q²/2C = ½CV² — connecting a charged and an uncharged capacitor always loses energy (heat/radiation).
keyPoints: C = Q/V; parallel plate C = ε0A/d (with dielectric: Kε0A/d).
Parallel: capacitances add; same V across all.
Series: reciprocals add; same Q on all.
Stored energy U = ½CV² = Q²/2C.
practiceQuestions: Q. Two 4 μF capacitors in series, then the pair in parallel with a 2 μF one — find total C. (2 marks) — series pair = 2 μF; total = 4 μF.
Q. How does C change if the plate separation halves? (1 mark) — doubles (C ∝ 1/d).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Master relation: I = neAvd — every numerical (current, drift speed, number density, area) comes from this one equation.
Trick 2: σ = ne²τ/m links conductivity to relaxation time τ; resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ) — quote for the 'why do metals conduct' question (large n).
Trick 3: Drift speed is tiny (~mm/s) yet the bulb glows instantly — because the ELECTRIC FIELD propagates near light speed; that one-liner is the favourite viva mark.
keyPoints: Current I = neAvd (n = charge-carrier density, vd = drift velocity).
Drift velocity is the small average velocity superimposed on random thermal motion.
σ = ne²τ/m; metals conduct because n is huge.
Current density J = σE (microscopic form of Ohm's law).
practiceQuestions: Q. Copper wire, n = 8.5 × 10^28 m^-3, A = 1 mm², I = 1.36 A — find vd. (3 marks) — vd = I/(neA) ≈ 1 × 10^-4 m/s.
Q. Why does current start instantly although vd is small? (1 mark) — the electric field is established through the circuit almost at light speed.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Resonance frequency one formula: f0 = 1/(2π√LC) — every LC numerical is a substitution; state 'XL = XC at resonance'.
Trick 2: At resonance: impedance = R (minimum), current maximum, power factor 1 — three consequences for the 3-mark answer.
Trick 3: LC oscillation analogy: energy shuttles between C (electric) and L (magnetic) like mass–spring between KE and PE; frequency same formula shape (ω = 1/√LC).
keyPoints: LC circuit oscillates with f0 = 1/(2π√LC).
At resonance inductive and capacitive reactances cancel.
Impedance is minimum (= R) and current maximum at resonance.
Energy alternates between the capacitor's field and the inductor's field.
practiceQuestions: Q. Find the resonant frequency of a 2 mH inductor with a 5 μF capacitor. (2 marks) — f = 1/(2π√(2e-3 × 5e-6)) ≈ 1.59 kHz.
Q. What is the phase difference between V and I at resonance? (1 mark) — zero (purely resistive circuit).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Equation first: hν = φ + KEmax — then the three laws: current ∝ intensity; KE depends on FREQUENCY not intensity; emission is instantaneous above threshold.
Trick 2: Threshold: ν0 = φ/h; stopping potential eV0 = KEmax = hν − φ — every numerical is two of these three lines.
Trick 3: Graph marks: KE vs ν is a straight line with slope h and x-intercept ν0 — draw it; the slope measures Planck's constant.
keyPoints: Photoelectric emission happens only above the threshold frequency.
Einstein's equation: hν = W0 + KEmax.
Maximum KE depends on frequency, not on intensity.
Stopping potential measures KEmax: eV0 = hν − W0.
practiceQuestions: Q. Work function 2 eV, light of 4 eV photon energy — find stopping potential. (2 marks) — KEmax = 2 eV → V0 = 2 V.
Q. Why does increasing intensity not increase KEmax? (1 mark) — intensity adds photons (more electrons), but each photon's energy hν sets the KE.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Truth tables in one line each — AND: 1 only when both 1; OR: 1 when any 1; NOT: inverts; NAND: NOT of AND (0 only when both 1); NOR: NOT of OR (1 only when both 0).
Trick 2: Universal gates: NAND and NOR can build every other gate — the 'why' mark; show NOT = NAND with both inputs joined.
Trick 3: Boolean identities that save time: A + A B = A; A + Ā = 1; (A B)' = Ā + B̄ (De Morgan) — most simplification questions die with De Morgan.
keyPoints: AND, OR, NOT are the basic gates; NAND, NOR are universal.
Output expressions: AND = A·B, OR = A + B, NAND = (A·B)', NOR = (A + B)'.
De Morgan's theorems convert between NAND/NOR forms.
XOR gives 1 for unequal inputs.
practiceQuestions: Q. Draw the truth table of a NAND gate. (2 marks) — 00→1, 01→1, 10→1, 11→0.
Q. Show how a NOR gate can work as NOT. (1 mark) — tie both inputs together: (A+A)' = Ā.
